query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys used at high temperatures, the development of locally ordered atomic clusters (i.e., short-range chemical order) governs both structural and chemical stability by reducing atomic mobility and preventing phase separation. This effect is further enhanced by buffering sublattice interactions (such as an oxygen sublattice in oxides) that can absorb strain and accommodate configurational fluctuations.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy nanoalloy initially synthesized as a nearly random, disordered solid solution with minimal pre-existing short-range order.
generation.intervention: Expose the nanoalloys to a high-temperature annealing protocol within an inert atmosphere, designed to activate atomic diffusion and allow for the spontaneous development of short-range chemical ordering.
generation.conditions: Annealing temperatures near (but below) the melting point for sufficient time; inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; alloy compositions similar either to rocksalt high-entropy oxides (e.g., (Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O) or metallic HEAs (e.g., Al0.1CrCoFeNi) where buffering effects (oxygen sublattice or atomic clustering under strain) are feasible.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of short-range ordered clusters that act as mediators by locally reducing atom mobility and absorbing mechanical strains. In oxide alloys, an underlying oxygen sublattice performs a similar buffering role.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, increased atomic mobility allows the atoms to rearrange into locally favorable configurations, forming clusters that lower the free energy barrier against further diffusion and phase transformation. This local ordering, potentially assisted by a buffering sublattice (such as oxygen in oxides), stabilizes the overall structure by mitigating extensive phase separation and maintaining a homogeneous phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Post-annealing, the nanoalloys should exhibit a measurable increase in indicators of short-range order (e.g., via pair correlation functions) and demonstrate enhanced structural stability—evidenced by improved resistance to phase separation or decomposition—compared to a baseline nanoalloy processed at lower temperatures (insufficient for ordering).
generation.baseline: Nanoalloys maintained at lower temperatures or processed under conditions that do not promote significant atomic rearrangement (thus retaining full configurational disorder).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold over a temperature range high enough to induce atomic diffusion but below the melting point, and for alloy compositions that possess the necessary elements to form either effective clustering or a buffering sublattice; compositions lacking these features or subjected to extreme thermal conditions may not follow the predicted trend.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of short-range ordering is anticipated, the precise temperature window and the quantitative magnitude of the stability enhancement remain uncertain and may vary with alloy composition and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy nanoalloy samples. Subject one set to high-temperature annealing (within the defined temperature window) intended to induce short-range ordering, while keeping the control set at a lower temperature where minimal ordering is promoted. Characterize both sets using advanced techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography to assess short-range order, and use X-ray diffraction (XRD) along with diffusion measurements to evaluate phase stability and atomic mobility.
measurements: Degree of short-range order via pair distribution function analysis or atom probe tomography
Phase composition and stability via XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in short-range order compared to the control set, or if the increased ordering does not correlate with improved structural stability (i.e., both sets show comparable levels of phase decomposition or degradation), then the hypothesis that enhanced short-range chemical order governs high-temperature stability is falsified.

(Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O: A rocksalt high-entropy oxide containing divalent Mn and Fe

Abstract: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Atomistic clustering-ordering and high-strain deformation of an Al0.1CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy

Abstract: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments.
